questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I am a really big fan of the US and the culture and wanted to experience it in a different way which can only be truly acheived by living in the country. I wanted to learn from the culture. The Americans are in general very outgoing which I think we as Danes can learn a lot from. I also wanted to improve my English and get more comfortable with it since I'm gonna use that for the rest of my working life. I was also really curious how they teach stuff in the US. They definitely managed to make in more tangible and interesting than in Denmark. This is because it's not as theoretical as in Denmark which is really nice in my opinion. I also wanted to develop as a person. I think putting myself out in a situation where I have to live in a new country where I don't know anyone is a really good way to develop as a person. I definitely have developed socially which is an important aspect in both my personal life, but also my working life. Nevertheless, I didn't chose the university based on the courses and if I could go back I would probably have chosen something more relevant to my studies. This is because it is a big gap now that I have to write my Master's Thesis that I haven't worked in the field for almost a year. Also because I did a lot of school work in the US and then it would have been better to do some school work which would have benefited me more.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
I did arrive during covid so I didn't get much help from the University. They didn't even have any introduction events, because of Covid. Some people would probably have prefered an official introduction and welcome.
Nevertheless, it wasn't a big problem for me.
I just asked the other students about the things I didn't know about which was a good way to engage with people.

questions.answer: Meal plans - very expensive food though. They had cooking facilities, but I had to buy pots and pans myself. This is in my opinion super stupid that every international student every year have to buy new pots and pans because they throw the old ones out.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: They have to buy pots, pans and everything else. It super good for social life. If you don't live on campus you definitely need a car in the US

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: If you want to get an A - it's very easy. It's very similar to high school. Teachers are really nice and want the student to be as good as possible. They give a lot of homeworks, but if you want to do good in the homework you can just show up for discussion sessions where they give you every answer.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
It was much more like high school. In Denmark I feel like it's my own responsibility to follow the classes. In the US the teachers take more care of the student to make sure the follow what's going on. 
Also during the classes the students are much more engaged and ask questions all the time in the US. In Denmark no one asked questions. They have the philosophy that there is no stupid questions in the US. This is not the case in Denmark where the teachers sometime clearly hint if a question is stupid.
